context: Wilde to Frank Harris, 20 June 1900, Pavillon d'Armenonville. The founding agreement of the whole Mr and Mrs Daventry business, three months before the assignment and four before the quarrel. Wilde had already sold options on the same plot to Mrs Brown-Potter, Sedger, Rehan, Nethersole and Smithers, which is what Harris later had to buy off.
quote:
Pavillon d’Armenonville, Bois de Boulogne, Paris. 20th June. 1900.

My dear Frank, It is quite understood that in the case of our collaboration in the play “Love is Law”, to our mutual satisfaction, all business transactions are to be directed by you — with the reservation of Mrs Brown-Potter’s rights, to be arranged by you —

Oscar Wilde
original_provenance: Read at HRC 2676, image 37 - one sheet of Pavillon D'ARMENONVILLE, Bois de Boulogne paper, sides 1 and 2, the whole letter. Signed 'Oscar Wilde' in full, as the September assignment is. A later hand has obliterated the one clause that matters. 'Mrs Brown-Potter's rights' is scored out under a dense scribble in soft grey pencil - a different medium from the black ink Wilde wrote in, and therefore not his pen. The words are still legible beneath at 3.2x, and the scribble stops exactly at them: 'reservation' above and 'to be arranged by you' below are untouched. So somebody went to this letter afterwards and struck out precisely the reservation of the rights that the October quarrel turned on. Whose pencil it is I cannot say and have not guessed. The volume prints the phrase as plain text with no indication that anything was struck — which is defensible if the editors read through it as I did, but it loses the fact of the deletion entirely. The words are kept in the quote here, unmarked, because they are Wilde's and the deletion is not; the deletion is recorded here instead of being encoded as his. Title: the play is “Love is Law”, in Wilde's own inverted commas, not underlined; the volume sets it in italic. Third instance of that conversion in this pass, after ‘Civilization — Cause and Cure’ (p. 1197) and ‘Her Second Chance’ (p. 1198). Quotation marks are his practice for a title and the printed italic is always the editor's. Emphasis: no underlines. The dateline '20th June. 1900.' is not underlined.
